title: Vestigial chirality from fluctuating loop currents on the kagome lattice
authors: Yin Shi, Xuande Bu, Sheng Meng
abstract: Multicomponent order can melt in stages, leaving a composite order after its primary constituents become short ranged. We study this possibility for commensurate three-$Q$ loop-current order on the kagome lattice. Large-scale cluster and parallel-tempering Monte Carlo simulations reveal direct and two-stage melting regimes in an effective fixed-amplitude sign model. In the latter regime, translation-sector domain walls proliferate before chirality-changing walls, restoring lattice translational symmetry while preserving long-range time-reversal-odd order. The primary $M$-point correlations are short ranged in this intermediate phase. The two-stage regime begins when the lowest-energy chirality-changing wall is only about $12$--$13\%$ more costly than a same-chirality translation wall. Finite-size scaling of a stable amplitude-resolved Ginzburg--Landau theory shows that the phase survives amplitude relaxation. Our results establish a quantitative domain-wall criterion for vestigial loop-current order and a fluctuation route to time-reversal symmetry breaking without long-range loop-current Bragg order. This separation provides a possible thermodynamic framework for time-reversal-odd responses recently reported above the critical temperature for conventional charge-density-wave ordering in kagome metals.
summary: This work investigates the complex phase transitions of loop-current order on the kagome lattice, predicting a two-stage melting process. Using advanced Monte Carlo simulations on effective field theories, the authors establish a quantitative criterion for a 'vestigial chiral phase.' This finding offers a theoretical mechanism explaining time-reversal-odd responses observed in materials above their primary charge-density-wave transition temperatures.
main_problem: The study investigates the possibility of a 'vestigial chiral regime' where a time-reversal-odd composite order persists after the primary, translation-breaking loop-current order melts.
main_result: The research establishes a quantitative domain-wall criterion for this vestigial order, suggesting a two-stage melting process that can provide a framework for time-reversal-odd responses above conventional CDW transitions.
method: The authors employed large-scale cluster and parallel-tempering Monte Carlo simulations on effective sign and soft-spin models derived from a coarse-grained Ginzburg-Landau theory.
model_or_system: The system models loop currents on the kagome lattice, using an effective Hamiltonian involving three symmetry-related M-point components ($\Phi_{ai}$). The analysis progresses from a sign model to a soft-spin model incorporating amplitude fluctuations.
key_observables: Loop-current order ($\chi$), bond order ($B$), specific heat ($c_V$), and the proliferation of domain walls (chirality-changing vs. translation walls).
important_parameters: The critical ratio $q = J_{\chi}A^4/K_{\Phi}$ governs the transition between regimes; the vestigial phase is predicted when the chirality-changing wall cost is only $12-13\%$ higher than the same-chirality wall.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on deriving an effective Hamiltonian by integrating out the bond field and assumes the stability of the vestigial phase can be confirmed by comparing domain-wall tensions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the coarse-graining process, different domain-wall classes (translation vs. chirality-changing), and real-space correlation functions ($C_s(r), C_{	au}(r)$) used to diagnose the distinct melting stages.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the general concept of multi-component order melting to applying it to the kagome lattice loop currents. It uses a sign model for initial analysis, extends to a soft-spin model for refinement, and concludes by establishing the quantitative domain-wall criterion for the vestigial phase.
why_interesting: The concept of vestigial order—where a symmetry-breaking feature persists after the primary order melts—is highly relevant to understanding complex phase diagrams in correlated materials, bridging concepts from statistical mechanics to electronic structure.
